claim: H3K27me2/3 covers approximately 7% of the N. crassa genome.
source: H3K27me2/3 covers approximately 7% of the N. crassa genome, including about 1000 fully-covered genes, all of which are transcriptionally quiescent (Jamieson et al., 2013; Galazka et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Jamieson et al., 2013; Galazka et al., 2016)

claim: H3K27me2/3 covers about 1000 fully-covered genes in N. crassa.
source: H3K27me2/3 covers approximately 7% of the N. crassa genome, including about 1000 fully-covered genes, all of which are transcriptionally quiescent (Jamieson et al., 2013; Galazka et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Jamieson et al., 2013; Galazka et al., 2016)

claim: All genes fully covered by H3K27me2/3 in N. crassa are transcriptionally quiescent.
source: H3K27me2/3 covers approximately 7% of the N. crassa genome, including about 1000 fully-covered genes, all of which are transcriptionally quiescent (Jamieson et al., 2013; Galazka et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Jamieson et al., 2013; Galazka et al., 2016)

claim: N. crassa has greater than 200 H3K27me2/3 domains.
source: The greater than 200 H3K27me2/3 domains, which range from 0.5 to 107 kb, are widely distributed throughout the genome but are enriched at subtelomeric regions (Jamieson et al., 2013), as also reported for other fungi (Schotanus et al., 2015; Dumesic et al., 2015; Studt et al., 2016; Connolly et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Jamieson et al., 2013)

claim: H3K27me2/3 domains in N. crassa range from 0.5 to 107 kb in size.
source: The greater than 200 H3K27me2/3 domains, which range from 0.5 to 107 kb, are widely distributed throughout the genome but are enriched at subtelomeric regions (Jamieson et al., 2013), as also reported for other fungi (Schotanus et al., 2015; Dumesic et al., 2015; Studt et al., 2016; Connolly et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Jamieson et al., 2013)

claim: H3K27me2/3 domains in N. crassa are enriched at subtelomeric regions.
source: The greater than 200 H3K27me2/3 domains, which range from 0.5 to 107 kb, are widely distributed throughout the genome but are enriched at subtelomeric regions (Jamieson et al., 2013), as also reported for other fungi (Schotanus et al., 2015; Dumesic et al., 2015; Studt et al., 2016; Connolly et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Jamieson et al., 2013; Schotanus et al., 2015; Dumesic et al., 2015; Studt et al., 2016; Connolly et al., 2013)

claim: Subtelomeric enrichment of H3K27me2/3 has been reported for other fungi.
source: The greater than 200 H3K27me2/3 domains, which range from 0.5 to 107 kb, are widely distributed throughout the genome but are enriched at subtelomeric regions (Jamieson et al., 2013), as also reported for other fungi (Schotanus et al., 2015; Dumesic et al., 2015; Studt et al., 2016; Connolly et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Schotanus et al., 2015; Dumesic et al., 2015; Studt et al., 2016; Connolly et al., 2013)

claim: Transplantation of eight three kb segments from a 47 kb H3K27me2/3 domain on LG VIL to his-3 locus did not induce H3K27me2/3.
source: H3K27me2/3 chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) followed by qPCR demonstrated the absence of de novo H3K27me2/3 within all eight segments when transplanted to either his-3 or csr-1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C

claim: Transplantation of eight three kb segments from a 47 kb H3K27me2/3 domain on LG VIL to csr-1 locus did not induce H3K27me2/3.
source: H3K27me2/3 chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) followed by qPCR demonstrated the absence of de novo H3K27me2/3 within all eight segments when transplanted to either his-3 or csr-1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C

claim: UK3-41 is an insertional translocation strain with an approximately 1.88 Mb segment of LG VR inserted into a distal position on LG VIL.
source: We first examined translocations that involved the H3K27me2/3 domain on LG VIL that we had dissected, starting with UK3-41, an insertional translocation strain that has an approximately 1.88 Mb segment of LG VR inserted into a distal position on LG VIL (Figure 1A).
evidence: Described in text and illustrated in Figure 1A

claim: In UK3-41, the region of LG VIL displaced from the chromosome end lost H3K27me2/3.
source: Interestingly, H3K27me2/3 ChIP-seq of UK3-41 showed an absence of H3K27me2/3 in the region that was displaced from the chromosome end (lost H3K27me2/3; indicated in orange in Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 1A

claim: The loss of H3K27me2/3 in UK3-41 suggests that normal methylation of the subtelomeric domain is position-dependent.
source: This result is consistent with our finding that transplantation of segments from this region did not induce methylation at his-3 or csr-1 and suggests that the normal methylation of this subtelomeric domain is position-dependent.
evidence: Inferred from ChIP-seq data and transplantation experiments

claim: OY350 is a quasiterminal translocation that transfers a distal segment of LG VIL to the end of LG IR.
source: To address this possibility, we utilized OY350, a quasiterminal translocation that transfers a distal segment of LG VIL to the end of LG IR (Figure 1B).
evidence: Described in text and illustrated in Figure 1B

claim: In OY350, the translocated LG VIL domain preserved its normal H3K27me2/3 distribution when placed adjacent to the adoptive telomere.
source: Analysis of OY350 by H3K27me2/3 ChIP-seq showed that the translocated LG VIL domain preserved its normal H3K27me2/3 distribution when placed adjacent to the adoptive telomere.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data for OY350

claim: H3K27me2/3 in the LG VIL domain depends on its proximity to a chromosome end.
source: This finding supported the hypothesis that H3K27me2/3 in this domain depends on its proximity to the chromosome end and suggested that this requirement is non-specific; the different chromosome end apparently substituted for the native one.
evidence: Inferred from OY350 ChIP-seq data showing preservation of H3K27me2/3 at adoptive telomere

claim: The requirement for proximity to a chromosome end for H3K27me2/3 is non-specific with respect to which chromosome end.
source: This finding supported the hypothesis that H3K27me2/3 in this domain depends on its proximity to the chromosome end and suggested that this requirement is non-specific; the different chromosome end apparently substituted for the native one.
evidence: Inferred from OY350 data showing H3K27me2/3 preservation at a different chromosome end

claim: Seven genome rearrangements independently showed de novo H3K27me2/3 at their new chromosome ends.
source: Striking examples of de novo H3K27me2/3 were independently observed in seven genome rearrangements at their new chromosome ends (Figure 1B–E and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C; marked in green).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figures 1B-E and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A-C

claim: Novel domains of H3K27me2/3 at new chromosome ends extended an average of approximately 180 kb into the new subtelomeric regions.
source: These novel domains of H3K27me2/3 extended an average of approximately 180 kb into the new subtelomeric regions.
evidence: Calculated from ChIP-seq data of translocation strains

claim: The H3K27me2/3 distribution on chromosomes unrelated to genome rearrangements was unaltered.
source: The H3K27me2/3 distribution on all chromosomes unrelated to the genome rearrangements was unaltered (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3

claim: Chromosome ends promote the deposition of H3K27me on neighboring chromatin.
source: Altogether, our survey of chromosomal translocations strongly suggests that chromosome ends promote the deposition of H3K27me on neighboring chromatin.
evidence: Inferred from multiple translocation experiments showing gain of H3K27me2/3 at new chromosome ends

claim: In ALS159, the shifted segment of LG VIR lost the H3K27me2/3 that was previously closest to the chromosome end.
source: Although the shifted segment lost the H3K27me2/3 that was previously closest to the chromosome end, the more internal H3K27me2/3 was unaffected by the translocation (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 1C

claim: In ALS159, the more internal H3K27me2/3 on LG VIR was unaffected by the translocation.
source: Although the shifted segment lost the H3K27me2/3 that was previously closest to the chromosome end, the more internal H3K27me2/3 was unaffected by the translocation (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 1C

claim: In OY329, most of the H3K27me2/3 on LG VIR was retained when inserted in the middle of LG III.
source: Similarly, when LG VIR was inserted in the middle of LG III in OY329 (Figure 1D), most of the H3K27me2/3 on LG VIR was retained.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 1D

claim: In OY329, the H3K27me2/3 that was originally closest to the telomere on LG VIR was lost.
source: Again, the H3K27me2/3 that was originally closest to the telomere was lost, however, consistent with the idea that subtelomeric H3K27me2/3 domains depend on their proximity to the chromosome ends.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data for OY329

claim: Subtelomeric H3K27me2/3 domains depend on their proximity to chromosome ends.
source: Again, the H3K27me2/3 that was originally closest to the telomere was lost, however, consistent with the idea that subtelomeric H3K27me2/3 domains depend on their proximity to the chromosome ends.
evidence: Inferred from multiple translocation experiments showing loss of subtelomeric H3K27me2/3 when moved away from chromosome ends

claim: In NM149, losses of H3K27me2/3 occurred in the most distal section of LG VR, but most H3K27me2/3 was retained.
source: Like the behavior of LG VIR in ALS159 and OY329, losses of H3K27me2/3 occurred in the most distal section of LG VR, but most H3K27me2/3 was retained, even when moved away from the chromosome end.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data for NM149

claim: In OY320, a large H3K27me2/3 domain on LG IIIR did not incur losses when shifted approximately 450 kb away from the chromosome end.
source: In addition, a large H3K27me2/3 domain on LG IIIR was shifted approximately 450 kb away from the chromosome end in OY320, yet it did not incur losses (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 1F

claim: Some H3K27me2/3 domains can be maintained when translocated to internal chromosomal sites.
source: Taken together, these findings demonstrate that some H3K27me2/3 domains can be maintained when translocated to internal chromosomal sites, i.e. some H3K27me domains appear to be position-independent.
evidence: Inferred from ChIP-seq data of multiple translocations showing retention of H3K27me2/3 at internal sites

claim: Some H3K27me domains appear to be position-independent.
source: Taken together, these findings demonstrate that some H3K27me2/3 domains can be maintained when translocated to internal chromosomal sites, i.e. some H3K27me domains appear to be position-independent.
evidence: Inferred from ChIP-seq data showing retention of H3K27me2/3 at internal chromosomal sites

claim: In a segmental duplication strain derived from OY329 crossed with Mauriceville, the duplicated chromosomal segments have distinct H3K27me2/3 profiles.
source: SNP-parsed H3K27me2/3 ChIP-seq showed that the duplicated chromosomal segments have distinct H3K27me2/3 profiles (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by SNP-parsed ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2B

claim: The previously subtelomeric H3K27me2/3 that was lost in OY329 did not return in the duplication strain.
source: The previously subtelomeric H3K27me2/3 that was lost in OY329 did not return in the duplication strain, nor was the loss in this region recapitulated on the native LG VIR of MV.
evidence: Supported by SNP-parsed ChIP-seq data of duplication strain

claim: The loss of H3K27me2/3 in OY329 was not recapitulated on the native LG VIR of Mauriceville in the duplication strain.
source: The previously subtelomeric H3K27me2/3 that was lost in OY329 did not return in the duplication strain, nor was the loss in this region recapitulated on the native LG VIR of MV.
evidence: Supported by SNP-parsed ChIP-seq data of duplication strain

claim: The loss of H3K27me2/3 in OY329 was not a result of trans-acting factors, but rather was a result of the translocation itself.
source: The independent behavior of these homologous segments suggests that the loss of H3K27me2/3 in OY329 was not a result of trans-acting factors, but rather was a result of the translocation itself, that is, it is a bona fide position effect.
evidence: Inferred from SNP-parsed ChIP-seq data showing independent behavior of homologous segments

claim: The loss of H3K27me2/3 in OY329 is a bona fide position effect.
source: The independent behavior of these homologous segments suggests that the loss of H3K27me2/3 in OY329 was not a result of trans-acting factors, but rather was a result of the translocation itself, that is, it is a bona fide position effect.
evidence: Inferred from SNP-parsed ChIP-seq data showing independent behavior of homologous segments

claim: The gain of H3K27me2/3 on LG VIL in OY350 coincided with reduced transcript levels relative to wild-type.
source: The gain of H3K27me2/3 on LG VIL in OY350, due to formation of a novel subtelomere, coincided with reduced transcript levels relative to wild-type (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq and ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 3A

claim: The loss of H3K27me2/3 on LG IR in OY350 was associated with an increase in transcript abundance compared to wild-type.
source: Conversely, the loss of H3K27me2/3 on LG IR in OY350, due to shifting the subtelomeric region, was associated with an increase in transcript abundance compared to wild-type (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq and ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 3B

claim: Analysis of seven translocation strains showed increases in gene expression at previously subtelomeric regions that lost H3K27me2/3.
source: Indeed, a comprehensive analysis of poly-A+ mRNA-seq data from all seven translocation strains showed increases in gene expression at previously subtelomeric regions that lost H3K27me2/3 and decreases in gene expression at novel subtelomeres that gained H3K27me2/3 (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data from seven translocation strains shown in Figure 3C

claim: Analysis of seven translocation strains showed decreases in gene expression at novel subtelomeres that gained H3K27me2/3.
source: Indeed, a comprehensive analysis of poly-A+ mRNA-seq data from all seven translocation strains showed increases in gene expression at previously subtelomeric regions that lost H3K27me2/3 and decreases in gene expression at novel subtelomeres that gained H3K27me2/3 (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data from seven translocation strains shown in Figure 3C

claim: Chromosomal rearrangements can cause marked changes in both H3K27me2/3 and gene expression of the affected regions.
source: These findings demonstrate that chromosomal rearrangements can cause marked changes in both H3K27me2/3 and gene expression of the affected regions.
evidence: Inferred from RNA-seq and ChIP-seq data of translocation strains

claim: Southern analysis of the tert strain using a (TTAGGG)n probe revealed major reductions in the hybridization signals.
source: Southern analysis of the tert strain using a (TTAGGG)n probe revealed major reductions in the hybridization signals and showed that the majority of telomere fragments present in wild-type were either undetectable or greatly reduced in the mutant (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by Southern blot data shown in Figure 4A

claim: The majority of telomere fragments present in wild-type were either undetectable or greatly reduced in the tert mutant.
source: Southern analysis of the tert strain using a (TTAGGG)n probe revealed major reductions in the hybridization signals and showed that the majority of telomere fragments present in wild-type were either undetectable or greatly reduced in the mutant (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by Southern blot data shown in Figure 4A

claim: N. crassa tert survivors have circular chromosomes.
source: Indeed, the tert genomic DNA, but not control DNA from a wild-type strain, supported amplification using the divergent primer pairs, confirming intra-chromosomal fusions (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by PCR data shown in Figure 4B demonstrating intra-chromosomal fusions

claim: With the exception of LG V, all chromosomes in the tert strain lost their subtelomeric H3K27me2/3 domains.
source: With the exception of LG V, which is unique in that one of its ends is capped with approximately 150 copies of the approximately 9 kb rDNA repeat (Butler and Metzenberg, 1990), all chromosomes lost their subtelomeric H3K27me2/3 domains, which typically extend tens of thousands of bp from their ends.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data of tert strain

claim: LG V is unique in that one of its ends is capped with approximately 150 copies of the approximately 9 kb rDNA repeat.
source: With the exception of LG V, which is unique in that one of its ends is capped with approximately 150 copies of the approximately 9 kb rDNA repeat (Butler and Metzenberg, 1990), all chromosomes lost their subtelomeric H3K27me2/3 domains, which typically extend tens of thousands of bp from their ends.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Butler and Metzenberg, 1990)

claim: Internal H3K27me2/3 domains were not noticeably altered in the tert strain.
source: Internal H3K27me2/3 domains were not noticeably altered (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: The losses of H3K27me2/3 ChIP signal observed in tert are not caused by chromosome degradation.
source: Sequencing of tert input DNA from the ChIP showed no reduction in coverage near the chromosome ends, confirming that the losses of H3K27me2/3 ChIP signal observed in tert are not caused by chromosome degradation.
evidence: Supported by sequencing data of tert input DNA showing no reduction in coverage

claim: Either (TTAGGG)n telomere repeats or linear chromosome ends are required for position-dependent domains of H3K27me2/3 in N. crassa.
source: We conclude that either (TTAGGG)n telomere repeats or linear chromosome ends are required for position-dependent domains of H3K27me2/3 in N. crassa.
evidence: Inferred from tert ChIP-seq data showing loss of subtelomeric H3K27me2/3

claim: Ectopic telomere repeats are sufficient to induce local H3K27me2/3 at the csr-1 locus.
source: H3K27me2/3 ChIP-qPCR demonstrated that ectopic telomere repeats are sufficient to induce local H3K27me2/3 at the csr-1 and his-3 loci (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 5A

claim: Ectopic telomere repeats are sufficient to induce local H3K27me2/3 at the his-3 locus.
source: H3K27me2/3 ChIP-qPCR demonstrated that ectopic telomere repeats are sufficient to induce local H3K27me2/3 at the csr-1 and his-3 loci (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: Insertion of (TTAGGG)8 triggered some H3K27 methylation at csr-1.
source: Even insertion of (TTAGGG)8 triggered some methylation and insertion of (TTAGGG)17 led to a high level of H3K27me2/3 at csr-1.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data

claim: Insertion of (TTAGGG)17 led to a high level of H3K27me2/3 at csr-1.
source: Even insertion of (TTAGGG)8 triggered some methylation and insertion of (TTAGGG)17 led to a high level of H3K27me2/3 at csr-1.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data

claim: ChIP-seq on the (TTAGGG)17 strain revealed new H3K27me2/3 peaks as far as 170 kb from the insertion site.
source: ChIP-seq on the (TTAGGG)17 strain revealed new peaks as far as 170 kb from the insertion site and the semi-continuous H3K27me2/3 domain spanned approximately 225 kb including 30 genes (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 2

claim: The semi-continuous H3K27me2/3 domain induced by (TTAGGG)17 spanned approximately 225 kb including 30 genes.
source: ChIP-seq on the (TTAGGG)17 strain revealed new peaks as far as 170 kb from the insertion site and the semi-continuous H3K27me2/3 domain spanned approximately 225 kb including 30 genes (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 2

claim: The size of the H3K27me2/3 domain induced by (TTAGGG)17 is comparable to the size of subtelomeric H3K27me2/3 domains that were lost in the tert strain.
source: This is comparable to the size of subtelomeric H3K27me2/3 domains that were lost in the tert strain.
evidence: Comparison of ChIP-seq data from (TTAGGG)17 strain and tert strain

claim: PcG proteins were initially discovered in Drosophila melanogaster as repressors of homeotic (HOX) genes during early embryogenesis.
source: PcG proteins were initially discovered in Drosophila melanogaster as repressors of homeotic (HOX) genes during early embryogenesis (Lewis, 1978) and play integral roles in the maintenance of cellular identity and differentiation in a variety of eukaryotes.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Lewis, 1978)

claim: PcG proteins play integral roles in the maintenance of cellular identity and differentiation in a variety of eukaryotes.
source: PcG proteins were initially discovered in Drosophila melanogaster as repressors of homeotic (HOX) genes during early embryogenesis (Lewis, 1978) and play integral roles in the maintenance of cellular identity and differentiation in a variety of eukaryotes.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about PcG proteins

claim: Dysfunction of the PcG system commonly leads to disease, including cancer.
source: Moreover, dysfunction of the PcG system commonly leads to disease, including cancer (Piunti and Shilatifard, 2016; Conway et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Piunti and Shilatifard, 2016; Conway et al., 2015)

claim: PcG proteins form two distinct histone-modifying complexes known as Polycomb Repressive Complex 1 and 2 (PRC1 and PRC2).
source: Biochemical work demonstrated that PcG proteins form two distinct histone-modifying complexes known as Polycomb Repressive Complex 1 and 2 (PRC1 and PRC2) (Müller et al., 2002; Wang et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Müller et al., 2002; Wang et al., 2004)

claim: PRC1 mono-ubiquitinates lysine 119 on histone H2A (H2AK119ub1) with its E3-ubiquitin ligase subunit, Ring1.
source: PRC1 mono-ubiquitinates lysine 119 on histone H2A (H2AK119ub1) with its E3-ubiquitin ligase subunit, Ring1, while PRC2 catalyzes mono-, di-, and trimethylation of histone H3 lysine 27 (H3K27me1/2/3) by its SET-domain component, EZH2 (Müller et al., 2002; Wang et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Müller et al., 2002; Wang et al., 2004)

claim: PRC2 catalyzes mono-, di-, and trimethylation of histone H3 lysine 27 (H3K27me1/2/3) by its SET-domain component, EZH2.
source: PRC1 mono-ubiquitinates lysine 119 on histone H2A (H2AK119ub1) with its E3-ubiquitin ligase subunit, Ring1, while PRC2 catalyzes mono-, di-, and trimethylation of histone H3 lysine 27 (H3K27me1/2/3) by its SET-domain component, EZH2 (Müller et al., 2002; Wang et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Müller et al., 2002; Wang et al., 2004)

claim: PRC2, but not PRC1, is widely conserved in eukaryotes, including the filamentous fungus Neurospora crassa.
source: PRC2, but not PRC1, is widely conserved in eukaryotes, including the filamentous fungus Neurospora crassa, but is absent in some simple eukaryotes such as the well-studied yeasts Saccharomyces cerevisiae and Schizosaccharomyces pombe (Jamieson et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Jamieson et al., 2013)

claim: PRC2 is absent in Saccharomyces cerevisiae and Schizosaccharomyces pombe.
source: PRC2, but not PRC1, is widely conserved in eukaryotes, including the filamentous fungus Neurospora crassa, but is absent in some simple eukaryotes such as the well-studied yeasts Saccharomyces cerevisiae and Schizosaccharomyces pombe (Jamieson et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Jamieson et al., 2013)

claim: In D. melanogaster, DNA regulatory regions known as Polycomb Response Elements (PREs) recruit PcG proteins to specific chromatin targets to maintain transcriptional silencing.
source: In D. melanogaster, DNA regulatory regions known as Polycomb Response Elements (PREs) recruit PcG proteins to specific chromatin targets to maintain transcriptional silencing (Steffen and Ringrose, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Steffen and Ringrose, 2014)

claim: Similar cis-acting elements to PREs have been detected in Arabidopsis thaliana.
source: Recently, similar cis-acting elements have been detected in Arabidopsis thaliana (Xiao et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Xiao et al., 2017)

claim: In vertebrates and other organisms, the mechanism by which PcG proteins are directed to particular loci is elusive.
source: In vertebrates and other organisms, however, the mechanism by which PcG proteins are directed to particular loci is elusive (Bauer et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Bauer et al., 2016)

claim: The control of H3K27 methylation is fundamentally different from that of epigenetic marks in constitutive heterochromatin.
source: We show that the control of H3K27 methylation is fundamentally different from that of epigenetic marks in constitutive heterochromatin.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data comparing H3K27 methylation with other epigenetic marks

claim: The genomic distribution of H3K27 methylation is much more plastic than that of H3K9 methylation.
source: Not only is the genomic distribution of H3K27 methylation much more plastic than that of H3K9 methylation (Jamieson et al., 2016; Mathieu et al., 2005; Deleris et al., 2012; Lindroth et al., 2008; Reddington et al., 2013; Hagarman et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2010), but also, unlike DNA methylation and methylation of histone H3K9, which are faithfully methylated de novo when introduced at arbitrary ectopic genomic sites (Miao et al., 1994; Selker et al., 1987), we show that H3K27 methylation is often position-dependent.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Jamieson et al., 2016; Mathieu et al., 2005; Deleris et al., 2012; Lindroth et al., 2008; Reddington et al., 2013; Hagarman et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2010)

claim: DNA methylation and methylation of histone H3K9 are faithfully methylated de novo when introduced at arbitrary ectopic genomic sites.
source: Not only is the genomic distribution of H3K27 methylation much more plastic than that of H3K9 methylation (Jamieson et al., 2016; Mathieu et al., 2005; Deleris et al., 2012; Lindroth et al., 2008; Reddington et al., 2013; Hagarman et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2010), but also, unlike DNA methylation and methylation of histone H3K9, which are faithfully methylated de novo when introduced at arbitrary ectopic genomic sites (Miao et al., 1994; Selker et al., 1987), we show that H3K27 methylation is often position-dependent.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Miao et al., 1994; Selker et al., 1987)

claim: H3K27 methylation is often position-dependent.
source: Not only is the genomic distribution of H3K27 methylation much more plastic than that of H3K9 methylation (Jamieson et al., 2016; Mathieu et al., 2005; Deleris et al., 2012; Lindroth et al., 2008; Reddington et al., 2013; Hagarman et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2010), but also, unlike DNA methylation and methylation of histone H3K9, which are faithfully methylated de novo when introduced at arbitrary ectopic genomic sites (Miao et al., 1994; Selker et al., 1987), we show that H3K27 methylation is often position-dependent.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing loss of H3K27me2/3 when regions are moved

claim: Telomere repeats underpin the observed position effect on H3K27me.
source: We further demonstrate that telomere repeats underpin the observed position effect on H3K27me by showing that loss of telomerase abolishes subtelomeric H3K27me2/3 and that artificial introduction of telomere repeats at interstitial sites trigger deposition of H3K27me2/3.
evidence: Inferred from tert deletion and ectopic telomere repeat experiments

claim: Loss of telomerase abolishes subtelomeric H3K27me2/3.
source: We further demonstrate that telomere repeats underpin the observed position effect on H3K27me by showing that loss of telomerase abolishes subtelomeric H3K27me2/3 and that artificial introduction of telomere repeats at interstitial sites trigger deposition of H3K27me2/3.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data of tert strain

claim: Artificial introduction of telomere repeats at interstitial sites triggers deposition of H3K27me2/3.
source: We further demonstrate that telomere repeats underpin the observed position effect on H3K27me by showing that loss of telomerase abolishes subtelomeric H3K27me2/3 and that artificial introduction of telomere repeats at interstitial sites trigger deposition of H3K27me2/3.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data of strains with ectopic telomere repeats

claim: Telomere repeats are necessary for subtelomeric H3K27me2/3.
source: That is, telomere repeats themselves are both necessary for subtelomeric H3K27me2/3 and sufficient to trigger ectopic H3K27 methylation at internal chromosomal sites.
evidence: Supported by tert deletion experiments showing loss of subtelomeric H3K27me2/3

claim: Telomere repeats are sufficient to trigger ectopic H3K27 methylation at internal chromosomal sites.
source: That is, telomere repeats themselves are both necessary for subtelomeric H3K27me2/3 and sufficient to trigger ectopic H3K27 methylation at internal chromosomal sites.
evidence: Supported by experiments showing H3K27me2/3 induction by ectopic telomere repeats

claim: Native N. crassa telomeres have an average of 20 repeats.
source: Native N. crassa telomeres have an average of 20 repeats (Wu et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Wu et al., 2009)
